bollymeter.basis: Nagesh Kukunoor's political thriller drew comparisons to prestige drama for its layered writing and committed performances from Atul Kulkarni and Priya Bapat, with critics noting its sharp depiction of Mumbai's political underworld.

seasons.review_body: City of Dreams arrived in May 2019 as one of Hotstar Specials' most ambitious original productions - a Hindi-language political thriller rooted in the corrupt machinery of Maharashtra politics. Director Nagesh Kukunoor, known for restrained character-driven cinema, brought that sensibility to an assassination attempt on a political patriarch, letting the family fissures that follow drive the narrative. Atul Kulkarni and Priya Bapat carried the weight of a show whose grounded portrayal of the compromises required to survive in the political arena set it apart from the typical streaming drama. The ten-episode run allowed the show room to develop its ensemble without rushing toward resolution.

Film Companion noted the show's political intrigue 'achieves lift-off a little too late in the game', but praised Priya Bapat and Siddharth Chandekar's screen presence in the sibling rivalry. The opening episode establishes the series' core dynamic - a political dynasty at war with itself - with clarity and confident direction from Nagesh Kukunoor.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# City Of Dreams S01E01: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The episode opens inside a mind trying to police itself. A voice reaches for Jung, for theory, for a name large enough to contain what is happening. Then the room gets louder. **Chas** is at the door. **John** is under pressure. Someone wants the bloody door opened, and the phrase carries more than plot mechanics. The supernatural door matters, but Chas is also forcing open the human one John keeps shut. The hour’s sharpest idea is clear: an abstract demon becomes more frightening once it has a child’s name attached to it.

## The Demon Has a Vocabulary Before It Has a Face

The episode begins in the head, a risky place to start. A speaker invokes Jung and calls the threat “Materialized psychisms,” turning inner disturbance into something that can stand in a room and push back. That choice gives the opening a specific texture. The danger first arrives as projection, as inner filth made physical, as something the mind has expelled and may have to reclaim.

That hook makes John’s problem intimate before the case has even formed. The language suggests a breach between the conscious and the unconscious, and the proposed solution is containment: take the “nasty little buggers” back. The writing is blunt enough to keep the scene from floating away into lecture. The Jung reference gives the premise a spine. “Nasty little buggers” drags it back into John’s rougher, uglier register.

The risk is front-loading concept before character. For a few minutes, the scene explains its rules while the emotional situation waits outside the door. Still, the concept has teeth. If the mind is the battlefield, every personal wound can become evidence. That matters once Chas arrives, because the episode stops treating theory as an object of interest and starts making it answer for damage.

John’s response also tells us plenty before the story spells anything out. He is irritated, cornered, and already defensive. The occult vocabulary may be elaborate, but his posture is practical. He knows what these things can cost. He also knows that naming a demon does not mean controlling it. That unease gives the opening its bite.

## A Door Opens, and the Past Walks In

“Open the bloody door, John” is the episode’s cleanest pressure line because it works as action and accusation. The door is a physical barrier in the scene. It is also the boundary John is trying to maintain around his mind, his history, and his guilt.

The argument between John and Chas works because it refuses politeness. Chas does not enter as a calm messenger with a neat case file. He pushes, questions, accuses, and drags private history into the open. The line about seven months of separation anchors the relationship rupture with useful economy. It tells enough. These two people have history, and the history is dirty.

That personal friction gives the supernatural premise a better engine. John can talk about demons and doors, but Chas arrives with a more embarrassing kind of haunting: consequences. Who slept with whom. Who left. Who knows what. Who still needs help anyway. The writing understands that exposition lands harder when it is being thrown like crockery.

The scene’s weakness is density. The middle stretch packs concept, argument, relationship damage, and urgent command into a small space. It has momentum, though some transitions feel more functional than elegant. The episode is sprinting toward the real wound. Once it gets there, the hour improves.

There is also a useful imbalance in the confrontation. John has the occult expertise, but Chas controls the emotional terrain. He knows which buttons to press because he helped build some of them. That keeps John from becoming a detached guide through supernatural procedure. He is being dragged into the case as a culprit, a resource, and maybe a last resort.

## Chas Refuses the Easy Spell

Chas’s most interesting contradiction is the episode’s best piece of character writing. He wants John involved because John can sense the shape of the unnatural. At the same time, he resists the lazy explanation that every terrible thing must be dark magic. That tension makes him more than a desperate messenger.

He is trying to make the crisis specific enough to act on while refusing to let John turn it into one of John’s familiar categories. Sometimes horror has a ritual. Sometimes a child is in a hospital bed and the doctors have no answer. Chas stands in that ugly middle space, demanding help while refusing comfort.

That choice prevents the episode from becoming a simple supernatural job offer. Chas does not arrive with a clean monster to kill. He arrives with uncertainty. He knows something is wrong. He knows John may be useful. He also knows that calling it magic too quickly might be another way of avoiding the ordinary cruelty of the world.

This is where the writing finds its grit. Chas’s anger has a purpose. It is a man trying to force meaning onto a situation that may not give him any. The episode uses that contradiction to sharpen the premise: John’s world may contain demons, but Chas will not let every tragedy wear horns.

The performance dynamic implied in the scene matters too. Chas’s urgency keeps interrupting John’s instinct to define the problem. John reaches for framework. Chas reaches for the patient. That clash gives the dialogue a lived-in hostility. They are arguing about magic, but the real subject is trust. Chas needs John and resents needing him. John wants distance and knows distance may be cowardice.

## Tricia Turns Theory Into Debt

The turn arrives with **Tricia**. Until then, the episode has operated through argument and concept. Once Chas says she is in a coma, the scene changes temperature. The abstraction collapses. Projection, unconscious doors, dark magic, separation, suspicion: all of it now has to stand beside a little girl in a hospital bed.

That is the right dramatic order. The opening gives the threat language. The Chas argument gives it friction. Tricia gives it cost. The doctors having no answers also keeps the case open without over-defining it. The episode plants clean questions: what caused the coma, why John, and what exactly will he find if he agrees to look?

Chas’s final ask is small on the surface: “Just come have a look at her. That’s all I’m asking.” The line works because it underplays the demand. He is not asking John to save the world in grand terms. He is asking him to show up. In a story built around doors, that request carries weight.

The limitation is that the episode excerpt ends on the ask rather than on a choice. That gives the opening chapter a strong hook, but not yet a full dramatic shape. It plants effectively. It does not completely pay off. For a premiere, that can work, provided the next move gives John’s response the weight this setup earns.

Tricia’s coma also clarifies the moral stakes without overexplaining the mythology. The episode does not need a full catalogue of symptoms yet. The image of a child beyond medical explanation is enough. It turns John’s expertise into debt. If he can help and refuses, his refusal becomes part of the harm. If he helps and fails, the case will expose the limits of the language he used so confidently at the start.

## The Verdict

“Episode 1” is a compact, jagged opener that works best when personal desperation interrupts supernatural theory. The Jung framing gives the premise a distinctive mental-horror angle, and the door imagery does useful work without becoming precious. The Chas and John confrontation carries the hour because it has history under the shouting, and Tricia’s coma turns the exchange from occult noise into obligation.

The score is held back by how much the opening has to explain in a short run of scenes. The conceptual language is intriguing, but the episode gains force when Chas drags the story out of John’s head and toward a hospital room. As a season starter, it plants clean questions and gives the central relationship enough damage to matter.

verdict.one_liner: A tense opener where supernatural theory only starts working once Chas makes the crisis painfully personal.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 deepened the Gaikwad family conflict while expanding the political canvas, maintaining the series' reputation for competent ensemble work even as some critics found the plotting more convoluted.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 returned in July 2021 with the Gaikwad family succession battle now fully in motion. Where the first season used the assassination attempt as a catalyst, the second spread its energy across factional infighting, coalition-building, and the personal costs of political ambition. The ten-episode format again served the story well, allowing Kukunoor to sketch supporting players with enough detail to make their betrayals register. Strong performances from the returning cast and a credible sense of the backroom deals that govern Indian political life remained the show's anchors, with Priya Bapat's female protagonist driving the central conflict without the narrative framing it as exceptional.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 widens the political map but adds complexity at the cost of some of the first season's tighter focus.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3 closed the series with its nine-episode finale run, delivering a resolution to the Gaikwad arc that rewarded viewers who had followed the family's trajectory across four years.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 concluded City of Dreams in May 2023 with a tighter nine-episode run that signalled the showrunners knew where the story needed to land. The political stakes from the earlier seasons converged as the Gaikwad family's internal war reached its endgame. Sachin Pilgaonkar's performance remained one of the series' consistent anchors, and the finale delivered enough resolution to justify the multi-season investment. The show never quite broke out of its niche audience, but over three seasons it established itself as one of the more seriously crafted Hindi-language political dramas available on Indian streaming platforms.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 3 contracts to nine episodes and sharpens the finale arc, delivering a more focused close than Season 2's wider sprawl.
